title: Classical-to-Quantum Transition in Blackbody Radiation Thermodynamics: Planck's Law without Statistical Assumptions
authors: J. Wang, G. Casati, G. Benenti
abstract: Inspired by Fermi's model of radiation-matter interaction, we investigate the classical dynamics of a closed, finite-energy system, in which matter is coupled to an electromagnetic field. We find that energy is progressively transferred to increasingly high-frequency field modes, so that the effective temperature of both matter and radiation approaches zero in the long-time limit - in sharp contradiction with the finite-temperature equilibrium assumed by classical blackbody thermodynamics. Requiring consistency with the Stefan-Boltzmann and Wien laws identifies a characteristic time $t_L$, at which both laws are simultaneously satisfied. Strikingly, classical spectra obtained for different energies and cavity sizes collapse onto the universal Planck distribution at $t_L$. We conjecture that quantum dynamical localization arrests the classical energy cascade at $t_L$, and that the Planck distribution emerges as a dynamical consequence of this arrest - without invoking any a priori statistical assumption.
summary: This work examines the classical dynamics of blackbody radiation, finding that the system's energy progressively leaks to high frequencies, causing temperatures to drop to zero, contradicting classical equilibrium. The authors propose that quantum dynamical localization arrests this classical energy cascade at a specific time $t_L$. At this moment, the classical energy spectrum spontaneously collapses onto the universal Planck distribution, suggesting a dynamical origin for quantum statistics.
main_problem: The paper investigates the classical-to-quantum transition in blackbody radiation thermodynamics, aiming to derive Planck's Law without relying on pre-existing statistical assumptions.
main_result: Classical dynamics fail to reach the finite-temperature equilibrium in the long-time limit, but at a characteristic time $t_L$, the classical spectra collapse onto the universal Planck distribution due to conjectured quantum dynamical localization.
method: The authors use numerical integration of the classical equations of motion for a coupled matter-field system, analyzing the time evolution of energy transfer and spectral density.
model_or_system: The model is a closed, finite-energy system consisting of matter (a charged particle) coupled to an electromagnetic field within a cubic cavity, supplemented by interactions with neutral particles on a 1D lattice.
key_observables: Energy transfer to high-frequency field modes, effective temperatures of matter and radiation, and the spectral energy-density $ho_\sigma(\omega, t)$.
important_parameters: The characteristic localization time $t_L$, which is found to be consistent with the Stefan-Boltzmann and Wien laws.
main_assumptions: The analysis is purely classical initially, and the emergence of Planck's law relies on the conjecture of quantum dynamical localization arresting the classical energy cascade.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate energy transfer over time, showing temperature decay in the classical limit, and demonstrate the collapse of classical spectra onto the Planck distribution at $t_L$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the classical Hamiltonian and simulates the energy cascade, showing temperature decay. It then identifies $t_L$ by requiring consistency with established laws, culminating in the conjecture that quantum localization causes the spectral collapse to the Planck distribution.
why_interesting: It provides a compelling, dynamical mechanism—quantum localization—to derive a cornerstone of thermodynamics (Planck's Law) from first principles of classical dynamics, bypassing the need for statistical ensembles.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic representation of our model. A single charged particle with charge e (shown in green) mediates the exchange of energy between the electromagnetic field within a cubic cavity and a chain of Np −1 neutral point particles (shown in black) interacting with their nearest neighbors.

FIG. 2. (a) The relaxation time (defined as the time to reach equipartition within 90% accuracy) for Np = 100, Etot = 2, and L = 20. The blue and red data points represent the relaxation time of the matter subsystem and the whole system, respectively. The best fitting of the latter suggests that it grows exponentially as Ce1.61|n|max with C ≈e10. (b) The effective temperatures of particles (to the left of the dotted line) and of field modes (to the right of the dotted line) for Np = 4000, Etot = 80, and L = 40, at various times from t = 3.2 × 105 to 1.2 × 108.

FIG. 3. Total field energy (a) and the average energy per particle (b) as a function of time. Curves correspond to Np = 5, 10, · · · , 4000. Here L = 20 and the conserved total energy is Etot = 0.02Np. Legend for (a) also applies to (b).

FIG. 5. (a) Comparison between the numerically com- puted field energy (red dots) and the prediction of the Stefan–Boltzmann law (blue dots) based on the field tem- perature at a given time. Blue triangles and squares show the Stefan–Boltzmann predictions obtained using, respectively, half and twice the value of Planck’s constant, highlighting the sensitivity of our results to its value. (b) The same as (a) but for the frequency at which the energy distribution peaks. The blue curves represent the predictions by Wien’s displacement law.

FIG. 6. Energy distribution of the radiation field at the local- ization time, tL, estimated when the classical system exhibits the Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann behaviors, for various values of Etot at L = 40 and various values of L with Etot = 80. Here T denotes the plateau temperature at time tL and the black dotted curve is for the universal function (3) given by the Planck distribution.
